hero.headline: Liverpool Agree £123 Million Deal for PSG Winger Bradley Barcola
hero.body:
Liverpool have completed negotiations with Paris Saint-Germain to sign winger Bradley Barcola in a deal worth up to £123 million. The 23-year-old French international will undergo a medical examination this weekend before finalising his move to Anfield.

The two clubs reached an agreement on the transfer structure following extended discussions, with Liverpool identifying Barcola as their primary summer target. The package is comprised of £106 million paid upfront, with an additional £17 million in add-ons dependent on individual and team performance.

Barcola has already agreed personal terms with Liverpool, with his representatives confirming the move last month. The winger will become the second-most expensive signing in the club's history, behind striker Alexander Isak, once he completes his medical and formalises the transfer.

At PSG, Barcola established himself as one of Europe's most promising attacking talents. His combination of pace and technical ability has drawn attention from elite clubs across the continent. The 23-year-old's performances for the French champions demonstrated the quality and potential that convinced Liverpool to commit significant resources to securing his signature.

The transfer reflects the current market reality for attacking players, with top-tier wingers commanding premium fees. Liverpool's decision to invest heavily in Barcola underscores their ambition to strengthen their squad as they pursue major honours domestically and in European competition.

The deal marks another significant piece of Liverpool's summer recruitment strategy. The Merseyside club have also brought in centre-back Ronald Araújo on loan from Barcelona, winger Víctor Muñoz from Osasuna, and defender Jérémy Jacquet from Rennes, whose £55 million transfer was agreed in January.

Barcola's arrival addresses a priority area for Liverpool as they prepare for the upcoming season. Manager Arne Slot will be keen to integrate the French winger into his squad, with hopes that he can make an immediate impact in the Premier League.

The medical examination scheduled for this weekend represents the final step before Barcola becomes an official Liverpool player. Once completed, the winger will join his new teammates at Anfield and begin preparations for his debut in English football.

Liverpool's investment in Barcola demonstrates their commitment to competing at the highest level. The club's recruitment team identified the PSG winger as someone capable of making a significant contribution to their attacking play, and negotiations were successfully concluded to bring him to Merseyside.

The transfer is expected to be formalised within days, pending the successful completion of Barcola's medical examination.

cards.headline: Trump Administration Announces Deal for US Control of Venezuelan Oil Assets
cards.body:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that his administration has reached an agreement with Venezuela's interim president Delcy Rodríguez that would give the United States majority control over 65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves in the South American country.

Trump stated the deal on his social media platform, noting that it was brokered through a partnership with private business interests. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth led the negotiations.

Rodríguez, Venezuela's interim president, characterized the arrangement as a measure intended to help revive her country's struggling economy. The Trump administration described the agreement as historic, representing a significant shift in US-Venezuelan energy relations.

The specific terms and mechanisms of the deal remain unclear. Trump's announcement did not provide details about how oil extraction, distribution, and revenue sharing would be structured, or the timeline for implementation.

This arrangement marks a notable departure from previous US approaches to Venezuela. The agreement involves working directly with private Venezuelan business entities that maintain connections to the Venezuelan government, a strategy that represents a change in diplomatic positioning.

The deal has sparked criticism from Venezuelan opposition groups. Reports of the US attempt to secure a substantial and long-term stake in Venezuela's energy reserves have generated significant backlash, with opponents describing the move as predatory and unconstitutional. Critics have characterized the arrangement as a land grab that prioritizes American interests over Venezuelan sovereignty.

The Venezuelan opposition's concerns center on the long-term implications of ceding control over the country's most valuable natural resource to foreign interests. They argue that such an agreement undermines national autonomy and resource management.

The agreement could have substantial economic implications for both nations, depending on implementation details and whether it leads to increased oil production and exports. Access to Venezuela's vast oil reserves positions American energy interests in a significant way as global energy markets remain a priority.

The Trump administration's willingness to directly engage with Venezuelan entities connected to the government represents a notable strategic shift. Previous administrations maintained greater distance from Venezuela's government and associated businesses, particularly during periods of political tension.

The deal comes at a time when the Trump administration has been actively reshaping US energy policy. However, this Venezuelan agreement contrasts sharply with recent administration actions in other energy sectors. In March, federal officials announced they would pay nearly $1 billion in taxpayer dollars to French energy firm TotalEnergies to cancel major offshore wind projects off the coasts of New York and North Carolina. That arrangement has prompted seven states to file lawsuits challenging its legality.

The Venezuelan oil agreement now awaits implementation as both countries work to structure the practical details of how American interests will gain access to and benefit from the nation's extensive proven reserves.

cards.headline: Iran faces fuel shortages as war and US blockade strain supply
cards.teaser: Long lines for gasoline have formed across Iran as the government struggles to meet fuel demand amid conflict and economic pressure.
cards.body:
The Iranian government is facing a fuel shortfall as the combined effects of ongoing war and a US blockade squeeze the country's oil supply. Long lines at gas stations have become common as authorities work to manage the shortage.

Officials are cautious about raising fuel prices at the pump, fearing that higher costs could trigger public unrest. The fuel crisis adds to mounting economic pressures on Iran as the government navigates both military conflict and international sanctions.

cards.headline: Military leaders advise against extending Iran operations
cards.teaser: A classified assessment warned that prolonged large-scale operations in the Middle East could weaken U.S. capabilities elsewhere.
cards.body:
Military leaders have advised against extending large-scale operations in the Middle East, according to a recent classified assessment. The evaluation warned that prolonged engagement in the region risks weakening U.S. military capabilities in other parts of the world.

The assessment was directed at Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as the administration weighs the scope and duration of ongoing operations. The warning reflects concerns about force readiness and strategic positioning as military resources remain concentrated in one theater.

cards.headline: CIA chief proposed summit between Trump, Putin, and Zelensky
cards.teaser: The director of the CIA has proposed a three-way summit involving the leaders of the United States, Russia, and Ukraine.
cards.body:
The CIA director suggested a summit meeting between former President Trump, Russian President Putin, and Ukrainian President Zelensky. The proposal comes as the war in Ukraine continues with no clear resolution in sight.

The diplomatic initiative represents an effort to bring the major parties to the conflict into direct negotiations. The proposal for a three-way summit has not yet been confirmed by any of the leaders involved.

cards.headline: Postal Service rule threatens mail voting access for millions ahead of midterms
cards.body:
The U.S. Postal Service is moving forward with a new regulation that would restrict mail-in voting despite court orders currently blocking its implementation. The rule, which the agency prepared to publish in the Federal Register, stems from a March executive order signed by Donald Trump.

Under the proposed regulation, states would be required to provide the federal government with lists of eligible voters and adopt new balloting procedures. The Postal Service would refuse to deliver mail-in ballots from states that fail to comply. The rule requires states to submit voter names and barcodes linked to mail-in ballots for federal elections to a federal database operated by the Department of Homeland Security.

Two federal courts, one in California and one in Massachusetts, have issued injunctions blocking the changes from taking effect. Nevertheless, the Trump administration is proceeding with implementation plans. According to the rule text, if courts lift the injunctions, the USPS intends to activate the system immediately, giving election officials time to comply before mail-in ballots are typically sent in September.

The federal government has sued 30 states and Washington D.C. for refusing to surrender voter lists. The USPS received more than 200,000 public comments during the rulemaking process on the proposed changes.

Nearly one in three Americans voted by mail in 2024. Mail voting expanded significantly during the pandemic and has remained popular across party lines. Legal experts and voting rights advocates have raised concerns about potential disenfranchisement, particularly for elderly and disabled Americans who depend on mail ballots.

Morris County in New Jersey has already announced plans to opt out of vote-by-mail services in response to the anticipated changes. The timing of the regulation has drawn scrutiny as the nation prepares for elections. Federal courts in multiple jurisdictions are weighing emergency motions and preliminary injunctions related to the rule.

The Postal Service has not publicly detailed the specific operational changes underlying the regulation or provided data on how many voters might be affected. Analysis from Vox suggests that Supreme Court precedent on election administration could influence whether the changes survive legal challenges. The Atlantic has criticized the Supreme Court's approach to evaluating factual claims in election-related cases.

The legal battle represents the latest conflict in ongoing disputes over election administration and ballot access. The outcome of the litigation could significantly reshape how Americans vote in upcoming elections. Any restrictions on mail ballot access would require millions of voters to change their voting plans, potentially creating logistical challenges for election officials managing in-person voting locations.

cards.headline: Federal Reserve Chair Warsh Faces Decision on Interest Rates as Inflation Persists
cards.teaser: Kevin Warsh must decide whether to raise rates if inflation continues, risking presidential criticism.
cards.body:
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh emphasized in his first major speech that controlling inflation is central to the Fed's mission, as price pressures remain stubbornly above the central bank's 2% target. While Warsh did not specify whether rates would rise in coming months, markets interpreted his remarks as signaling potential rate increases ahead.

The decision puts Warsh in a difficult position, as raising rates may conflict with President Trump's calls for rate cuts. Warsh has set a high bar for keeping rates unchanged, suggesting the Fed will act if economic conditions warrant tighter monetary policy to combat persistent inflation.

hero.headline: China reports 261 foreigners from 23 countries missing after Tibet flood
hero.body:
A glacier collapse and subsequent flooding on the Nepal-Tibet border has killed at least 543 people, with more than 1,500 missing across both countries. Chinese authorities disclosed that 261 of the 558 people missing in Gyirong County, Tibet are foreign nationals from 23 countries, offering rare detail about the disaster on the Chinese side of the border.

The catastrophic flooding occurred near Mount Kailash, a sacred mountain that draws pilgrims from across Asia. Many of those affected were international visitors in the region for guided treks, work projects, or religious pilgrimages. Thousands have been rescued by helicopter, though rescue efforts have faced obstacles from difficult terrain and concerns about additional flooding.

Nepal has reported the highest death toll, with 538 deaths confirmed and 977 people missing. Nepali authorities said 3,253 people have been rescued by helicopter, and more than 150 injured have been taken to hospitals in Kathmandu and surrounding districts. The missing on the Nepali side include 113 Nepali tourists, 85 military and police personnel, and 161 residents from the Rasuwa district.

India reported 288 Indian nationals unaccounted for, including 73 people working on a power project. Many Indian tourists were on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, considered a sacred site for Hindus.

Other countries with significant numbers of missing citizens include Ukraine with 55 people missing, the United States with 90 unaccounted for, Malaysia with 51, Australia with 39, and Britain with 33. Canada, South Korea, Singapore, Germany, Russia, South Africa, Latvia, Japan, and New Zealand each reported missing citizens in the single digits to low double digits. Smaller numbers of missing people have also been reported from France, Belgium, Spain, Italy, Kazakhstan, Portugal, Ireland, the Netherlands, and several other countries.

Rescue operations have faced challenges beyond terrain. A group of approximately 100 people became trapped in a tunnel at a hydropower project swamped by the flooding. Rescue teams had to suspend operations temporarily when a debris dam burst its banks, creating risks of fresh flooding and forcing residents to rush up hillsides to escape possible river surges.

Chinese state media has provided limited information about the disaster on the Chinese side of the border, with footage becoming difficult to find on China's censored internet. The announcement about foreign nationals represents one of the more detailed updates from Chinese officials since the flooding began. China's foreign ministry noted that nearly 100 Chinese citizens were also missing on the Nepal side of the border.

The death toll and missing numbers may vary as rescue efforts continue and data collection methods differ among various agencies and countries.

cards.headline: Iran faces fuel shortages as war and US blockade strain supply
cards.teaser: Long lines for gasoline have formed across Iran as the government struggles to meet fuel demand amid conflict and economic pressure.
cards.body:
The Iranian government is facing a fuel shortfall as the combined effects of ongoing war and a US blockade squeeze the country's oil supply. Long lines at gas stations have become common as authorities work to manage the shortage.

Officials are cautious about raising fuel prices at the pump, fearing that higher costs could trigger public unrest. The fuel crisis adds to mounting economic pressures on Iran as the government navigates both military conflict and international sanctions.

cards.headline: Iceland votes against restarting European Union membership talks
cards.teaser: Icelanders rejected a government proposal to resume negotiations on joining the European Union, according to broadcaster RUV.
cards.body:
Icelandic voters rejected the government's proposal to resume accession talks with the European Union in a referendum. According to public broadcaster RUV, the no camp secured 52.5% of the vote, with the yes camp receiving 47.5%. Only a small number of ballots remained to be counted at the time of the report.

The referendum result means Iceland will continue operating outside the EU framework. The vote concludes the current government's push to reconsider the country's relationship with the bloc.

cards.headline: Zambian opposition leader charged with treason
cards.teaser: A prominent opposition leader in Zambia has been charged with treason after previously seeking refuge at a UN building.
cards.body:
Zambian authorities have charged opposition leader Mundubile with treason. Mundubile had previously gone into hiding at a United Nations building in the capital, Lusaka.

The treason charge represents a significant escalation in tensions between the government and opposition forces in Zambia. The case is likely to draw international attention to political conditions in the southern African nation.

cards.headline: Russian strike on Ukraine ammunition depot kills 37
cards.teaser: A Russian attack on a Ukrainian weapons storage facility triggered waves of explosions in one of the deadliest strikes this year.
cards.body:
A Russian strike on a weapons depot near Kyiv killed at least 37 people, making it one of the deadliest attacks on Ukraine this year. The strike triggered multiple explosions at the ammunition storage facility, complicating rescue and recovery efforts as emergency teams worked at the site.

The attack occurred during an intense 72-hour period of near-constant Russian drone strikes across Ukraine. An investigation has begun into the weapons storage facility's location near a residential area, with hundreds of people evacuated from the vicinity.

cards.headline: Deportees describe treatment by US immigration authorities during expulsion to Liberia
cards.teaser: Ten people deported to Liberia said they witnessed what they described as abusive or violent treatment by ICE during months in detention.
cards.body:
Ten deportees sent to Liberia recounted what they called abusive or violent treatment by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials. They said they spent months in detention before being sent to a nation where they had no ties.

The deportees described their experiences during the expulsion process and their treatment while held by ICE. Several said they were sent to Liberia despite having no connections to the country.

cards.headline: Far-right party poised to win German state election
cards.teaser: The Alternative for Germany is expected to take power in a state election, raising concerns about intelligence sharing.
cards.body:
The Alternative for Germany is expected to win an upcoming state election. German state and federal officials are taking steps to limit the party's access to sensitive intelligence if it gains power.

The potential victory has prompted authorities to reassess intelligence-sharing protocols with state governments. Federal leaders are concerned about the security implications of a far-right party controlling a state administration and obtaining classified information.

cards.headline: Storm leaves tens of thousands without power in San Antonio as Texas heat continues
cards.teaser: More than 50,000 San Antonio residents remain without electricity after a powerful storm swept through the city.
cards.body:
Thousands of residents in San Antonio face days without power after a severe storm damaged electrical infrastructure across the city. More than 50,000 people remain without electricity as CPS Energy works to restore service. The outages come as Texas experiences intense summer heat, raising concerns about health risks for those without air conditioning.

City officials and CPS Energy have shared joint recovery efforts, with crews clearing storm damage throughout affected neighborhoods. West Side residents and those in Alamo Heights have begun cleanup efforts, removing debris and assessing property damage. The scale of the destruction suggests power restoration could take several more days in some areas.

---

Note: The additional source material provided relates to unrelated international stories (migrant crisis in Ceuta, Nepal-Tibet floods, and other global news) and does not contain information about the San Antonio power outages. The original card text has been retained unchanged.

cards.headline: Medicare pilot program limits GLP-1 discount access for some seriously ill patients
cards.teaser: A new Medicare program offers discounted GLP-1 drugs for $50 a month, but eligibility rules exclude many patients with severe illnesses.
cards.body:
Medicare launched a pilot program allowing some seniors to access GLP-1 medications for as little as $50 per month. The initiative aims to reduce costs and simplify the process for older Americans seeking these drugs, which are used to treat diabetes and for weight management.

However, the program excludes many patients with serious health conditions from receiving the discounted pricing. This means some of Medicare's sickest beneficiaries—those who may benefit most from these medications—will not qualify for the reduced rates under the pilot's eligibility restrictions.

cards.headline: Tariffs strain small businesses as Ohio comic book store owner grapples with costs
cards.teaser: A comic book store owner in Ohio faces financial pressure from tariffs more than a year after their introduction.
cards.body:
Tariffs imposed by the Trump administration continue to affect small businesses across the country, including a comic book store owner in Ohio. More than a year after the first round of tariffs took effect, retailers are still dealing with the fallout from ongoing trade disputes.

The comic book industry depends on imported products, from books printed overseas to collectibles and merchandise made abroad. Small retailers operating on tight margins struggle to absorb sudden cost increases without passing them on to customers, reflecting broader concerns among independent business owners about how trade policy impacts their bottom line.

cards.headline: NASA launches new space telescope to survey planets beyond solar system
cards.teaser: A tour-bus-sized telescope lifted off to search for planets and study cosmic phenomena.
cards.body:
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sunday morning, beginning its journey to deep space. The $4.3 billion observatory is designed to identify more than 100,000 planets beyond our solar system and search for clues about planet formation.

The mission survived two rounds of proposed budget cuts before reaching launch. The tour-bus-sized telescope will travel about a million miles into space, equipped with advanced technology to help scientists unlock secrets about the universe and study distant exoplanets.

cards.headline: Nepal issues fresh flood warnings after river levels rise
cards.teaser: Authorities urged residents in flood-affected districts to stay alert as the Bhotekoshi River reached concerning levels.
cards.body:
Nepal's authorities issued fresh flood warnings on Sunday as water levels rose in the Bhotekoshi River, urging residents in affected districts to remain on high alert. The alert comes as communities continue recovering from recent devastating floods across the country.

Delivery of aid to flood survivors has become increasingly difficult, with blocked roads and monsoon weather hampering efforts to distribute food, shelter, and emergency hygiene supplies to those in need.

cards.headline: Iceland votes against resuming EU membership talks
cards.teaser: A majority of Icelandic voters rejected the government's proposal to restart negotiations on joining the European Union.
cards.body:
Iceland voted against restarting EU accession talks in a close referendum, with 52.8 percent of voters rejecting the government's proposal according to public broadcaster RUV. The result halts the current effort to resume membership negotiations with the bloc.

The vote reflects deep divisions within Iceland over the country's relationship with Europe. Those supporting EU membership cite potential economic gains and closer ties to European markets, while opponents argue Iceland can better protect its interests—particularly regarding fisheries—by remaining independent outside the EU.

cards.headline: Treasury Department Denies Credentials to Reporters for G20 Finance Meeting
cards.teaser: Specific journalists from major outlets were not granted access to cover the financial leaders' meeting in North Carolina.
cards.body:
The Treasury Department barred specific reporters from The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and Bloomberg from covering next week's G20 finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. The reporters were not granted credentials to attend the gathering of financial leaders.

The decision to exclude journalists from major financial news organizations represents an unusual restriction on press access to an international economic summit. The meeting will bring together finance ministers and central bank governors from the world's largest economies.

cards.headline: Morgan Stanley Analyzes SpaceX's $100 Billion Louisiana Spaceport Investment
cards.teaser: The investment bank examined the broader implications of SpaceX's planned buildout in Louisiana.
cards.body:
Morgan Stanley has released analysis on SpaceX's planned $100 billion investment in Louisiana to build what would become the world's largest spaceport. The facility is designed to support Starship operations and represents one of the largest infrastructure investments in the space sector.

Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry framed the project as positioning the state as America's next frontier, reflecting a broader shift in space industry development toward the South.

cards.headline: Freedom Fuel Owner Faces Lawsuit Over Unpaid Gas Supplier Charges
cards.teaser: A lawsuit alleges the gas station chain promoted by Trump did not pay nearly $4 million for fuel.
cards.body:
A supplier has filed a lawsuit against Freedom Fuel's owner, claiming approximately $4 million in gasoline charges went unpaid. The gas stations gained attention after President Trump promoted them for their low prices.

The legal action suggests the discount pricing may have been achieved by not paying suppliers in full. Freedom Fuel locations in South Jersey had previously accumulated significant fines before receiving White House promotion.

cards.headline: Start-ups Rebrand Customer Service Roles as Forward-Deployed Workers
cards.teaser: Companies are using military-derived terminology to describe positions helping clients set up AI tools.
cards.body:
Technology start-ups are using the term "forward-deployed" to describe customer-facing workers who help clients implement artificial intelligence tools. The military-derived language reframes positions traditionally viewed as customer service or support work.

As organizations increasingly seek human assistance to configure and deploy AI systems, start-ups have created specialized roles combining technical expertise with direct customer interaction. The new terminology elevates how these positions are perceived and communicated.

cards.headline: Swiss Banking Regulator Warns Against Excessive Rules
cards.teaser: The incoming Swiss banking chief cautioned about the risks of regulatory over-reach in the financial sector.
cards.body:
The incoming head of Swiss banking regulation issued a warning against regulatory over-reach in the financial services industry. The statement addresses ongoing debates about the appropriate level of oversight for banking institutions.

Switzerland's banking sector remains a significant part of the country's economy and global financial system. The regulator's comments suggest a preference for balanced oversight that maintains stability without imposing excessive compliance burdens on financial institutions.

hero.headline: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope delivered to launch pad for Sunday launch
hero.body:
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope and its SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket have arrived at the launch pad at Kennedy Space Center in Florida ahead of a scheduled Sunday liftoff at 7:26 a.m. ET. The mission represents the next major step in NASA's effort to unlock fundamental mysteries about the universe.

The Roman Space Telescope is designed to search for exoplanets and investigate dark energy, dark matter, and the structure of the cosmos. With a 300-megapixel infrared camera, the telescope will offer the same sharpness as the Hubble Space Telescope but with a field of view at least 100 times larger. Each image will capture a patch of sky approximately 1.5 times the apparent size of a full moon.

The observatory will travel one million miles into deep space to reach Lagrange Point 2, where it will operate in the same orbit as the James Webb Space Telescope, though the two will remain far apart. Unlike the deep, focused observations made by other telescopes, Roman will conduct wide-field surveys that allow astronomers to study large portions of the universe simultaneously.

Named after Nancy Grace Roman, NASA's first chief astronomer who played a crucial role in planning the Hubble Space Telescope, the new observatory carries a specialized instrument called a coronagraph. This device blocks glare from stars, making it easier to photograph planets around them in detail.

The telescope project represents years of development. The need was conceived at the end of the last century, with development beginning in 2016 and full project approval coming in 2020. Julie McEnery, NASA's senior project scientist for the Roman mission, explained that one key motivation stemmed from discoveries about the universe's expansion. "One of the motivations for Roman was the discovery that our universe is not just expanding, but that expansion is accelerating," she said.

The $4.3 billion project survived two rounds of proposed White House budget cuts before finally reaching the launch pad. Congress rejected a 2025 proposal to terminate the Roman project, restoring NASA's 2026 funding to $24.4 billion.

Once operational, images from Roman will arrive in early 2027 after months of calibration and testing. NASA expects to make the imagery immediately public, allowing professional researchers and amateur astronomers unprecedented opportunities for analysis. The telescope's initial five-year mission could extend to ten years.

Roman will work alongside existing telescopes to provide comprehensive views of the cosmos. While Hubble and Webb can conduct detailed follow-up observations, Roman's panoramic images will uncover interesting targets and provide context around objects observed by other telescopes.

This launch marks the final flight of SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket as the company phases out older rocket models to focus on Starship development.

cards.headline: Apple schedules September 9 event for iPhone 18 launch
cards.teaser: Apple confirmed its next major product event will take place September 9, marking the first major launch under new CEO Ternus.
cards.body:
Apple has confirmed it will hold its next major product event on September 9, where the company is expected to unveil the iPhone 18 lineup. The event marks the first major product launch under Apple's new CEO following recent leadership changes.

Reports indicate Apple is planning to release the iPhone 18 Pro with new features and capabilities. Preorders for the new iPhone models are expected to begin shortly after the announcement. Apple is also reportedly working on a foldable iPhone as part of its future product roadmap.

cards.headline: Sony Music and Warner sue AI company Anthropic over copyright infringement
cards.teaser: Major music labels filed a lawsuit against Anthropic, accusing the AI company of intellectual property theft.
cards.body:
Sony Music and Warner Chappell have sued Anthropic in federal court in California, claiming the AI company infringed on "tens of thousands" of copyrighted musical works. The labels are seeking up to $150,000 in damages per work, plus an additional $25,000 for each instance where identifiable copyright information was removed.

The lawsuit represents one of the music industry's most expansive legal actions against an AI company, focusing on allegations of systematic intellectual property theft through illegal piracy.

cards.headline: Fifth grader becomes co-author of chemistry paper after creating new molecule
cards.teaser: A ten-year-old student in Kansas City co-authored a published chemistry paper after assembling atoms in science class.
cards.body:
A fifth-grade student in Kansas City became a co-author of a published chemistry paper after creating a molecule during a science class exercise. The student clicked together ball-and-stick atom models and asked her teacher if she had made a real molecule.

The teacher photographed the molecular structure and sent it to a chemistry professor for verification. At age ten, the student became a co-author on the resulting academic paper documenting the discovery. The case demonstrates how classroom activities can lead to legitimate scientific contributions.

cards.headline: Leaked footage shows EA's canceled Iron Man game
cards.teaser: Early gameplay footage from EA Motive's Iron Man game leaked online, prompting EA to acknowledge the unplanned disclosure.
cards.body:
Footage from EA Motive's Iron Man game leaked online after four years without official updates on the project. The leaked material shows gameplay features including destructible environments, flying mechanics, and other elements of the superhero game in development.

EA responded to the leak by stating the disclosure did not go as planned. The footage reveals Iron Man's return in video game form with what observers described as impressive visuals and gameplay systems. EA Motive has been working on the Marvel title, though no official release date has been announced.

cards.headline: Venture capitalist Vijay Pande launches smaller biotech fund after leaving Andreessen Horowitz
cards.teaser: Former head of Andreessen Horowitz's biotech practice started a new AI-focused venture fund with a more selective investment approach.
cards.body:
Vijay Pande has left Andreessen Horowitz's $4 billion biotech practice to launch VZVC, a smaller AI-native venture fund. The new firm operates with a more selective investment strategy, deliberately avoiding the high volume approach of his previous role.

Pande believes biology is transitioning from discovery-driven science to an engineering discipline, a shift powered by artificial intelligence advances. He argues that open, shared datasets—rather than proprietary ones—will be key to AI's ability to transform medicine, though he acknowledges that clinical trials remain prohibitively expensive.

cards.headline: European tech conference focuses on AI control and human agency
cards.teaser: Attendees at the TechBBQ conference in Europe repeatedly discussed questions about who controls artificial intelligence systems.
cards.body:
Investors, founders, and operators from across Europe gathered at the annual Nordic TechBBQ conference, where discussions centered on questions of control and human agency over artificial intelligence. The recurring theme reflected growing concerns about AI governance in the technology sector.

Participants at the conference examined how humans can maintain meaningful control as AI systems become more powerful and widely deployed. The focus on agency and oversight highlights ongoing debates in Europe about regulating and directing AI development.

hero.headline: Liverpool Agree £123 Million Deal for PSG Winger Bradley Barcola
hero.body:
Liverpool have completed negotiations with Paris Saint-Germain to sign winger Bradley Barcola in a deal worth up to £123 million. The 23-year-old French international will undergo a medical examination this weekend before finalising his move to Anfield.

The two clubs reached an agreement on the transfer structure following extended discussions, with Liverpool identifying Barcola as their primary summer target. The package is comprised of £106 million paid upfront, with an additional £17 million in add-ons dependent on individual and team performance.

Barcola has already agreed personal terms with Liverpool, with his representatives confirming the move last month. The winger will become the second-most expensive signing in the club's history, behind striker Alexander Isak, once he completes his medical and formalises the transfer.

At PSG, Barcola established himself as one of Europe's most promising attacking talents. His combination of pace and technical ability has drawn attention from elite clubs across the continent. The 23-year-old's performances for the French champions demonstrated the quality and potential that convinced Liverpool to commit significant resources to securing his signature.

The transfer reflects the current market reality for attacking players, with top-tier wingers commanding premium fees. Liverpool's decision to invest heavily in Barcola underscores their ambition to strengthen their squad as they pursue major honours domestically and in European competition.

The deal marks another significant piece of Liverpool's summer recruitment strategy. The Merseyside club have also brought in centre-back Ronald Araújo on loan from Barcelona, winger Víctor Muñoz from Osasuna, and defender Jérémy Jacquet from Rennes, whose £55 million transfer was agreed in January.

Barcola's arrival addresses a priority area for Liverpool as they prepare for the upcoming season. Manager Arne Slot will be keen to integrate the French winger into his squad, with hopes that he can make an immediate impact in the Premier League.

The medical examination scheduled for this weekend represents the final step before Barcola becomes an official Liverpool player. Once completed, the winger will join his new teammates at Anfield and begin preparations for his debut in English football.

Liverpool's investment in Barcola demonstrates their commitment to competing at the highest level. The club's recruitment team identified the PSG winger as someone capable of making a significant contribution to their attacking play, and negotiations were successfully concluded to bring him to Merseyside.

The transfer is expected to be formalised within days, pending the successful completion of Barcola's medical examination.

cards.headline: Filip Hrgovic Stuns Moses Itauma to Win World Heavyweight Title
cards.teaser: British heavyweight Moses Itauma lost his bid to become world champion after an unexpected defeat by Filip Hrgovic at London's O2 Arena.
cards.body:
Filip Hrgovic claimed the IBF world heavyweight title with a ninth-round stoppage of Moses Itauma at London's O2 Arena. The 34-year-old Croatian made a remarkable comeback after being dropped in the second round, as the 21-year-old Briton initially dominated with speed and powerful combinations through the early rounds.

Itauma's stamina faded dramatically in the latter stages of round eight, and Hrgovic seized the opportunity with renewed aggression. Unable to withstand the onslaught in the ninth round, Itauma was stopped as he retreated against the ropes. Hrgovic's victory marks him as the first Croatian to win a world heavyweight title and denies Itauma the chance to become the second-youngest champion in the division's history.

cards.headline: Tottenham Close to Signing Iliman Ndiaye as Richarlison Nears Everton Move
cards.teaser: Tottenham are in advanced negotiations to sign Iliman Ndiaye from Everton while Richarlison is set to move to Everton in separate talks.
cards.body:
Tottenham Hotspur are in advanced talks to sign winger Iliman Ndiaye from Everton. The negotiations form part of separate discussions that would see Richarlison move in the opposite direction, returning to Everton.

The transfer activity reflects both Premier League clubs reshaping their attacking options through the deal.

cards.headline: England Bowled Out for 208, Set Pakistan 389 to Win Second Test
cards.teaser: Josh Tongue was run out by Pakistan captain Babar Azam to end England's innings at 208, setting Pakistan a target of 389 runs at Lord's.
cards.body:
Josh Tongue was brilliantly run out by Pakistan captain Babar Azam for 12 runs, bringing England's second innings to a close at Lord's. The dismissal ended England's resistance and set Pakistan a target of 389 runs to win the second Test match.

Pakistan now face a substantial chase at the historic London venue as they pursue victory in the second Test.

cards.headline: Everton Cancel Harrison Armstrong Transfer After Fan Opposition
cards.teaser: Everton called off a proposed deal to sell midfielder Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest following supporter backlash.
cards.body:
Everton have called off a proposed transfer of midfielder Harrison Armstrong to Nottingham Forest following supporter backlash. Forest had made a reported £40m bid for the 19-year-old player.

Manager David Moyes indicated he preferred to keep Armstrong, stating the club cannot afford to lose key players. Armstrong featured for the full 90 minutes in Everton's recent 1-1 draw at Bournemouth before the transfer was abandoned.

cards.headline: Djurgardens Sign Abdul Abdulmalik for Record National League Fee
cards.teaser: Swedish club Djurgardens agreed a National League record fee exceeding £1.5 million to sign winger Abdul Abdulmalik from Boreham Wood.
cards.body:
Djurgardens have agreed a record fee for a National League transfer, signing winger Abdul Abdulmalik from Boreham Wood for a sum exceeding £1.5 million. The Swedish club's offer surpasses the previous record for a player moving from English football's fifth tier.

Abdulmalik's move represents a significant deal for Boreham Wood and highlights the growing market for National League talent among European clubs.

cards.headline: Arthur Fery Loses ATP Tour Final in Straight Sets
cards.teaser: Britain's Arthur Fery fell short of his first ATP Tour title with a straight-set defeat to Ignacio Buse in the Winston-Salem Open final.
cards.body:
Arthur Fery's maiden ATP Tour final ended in disappointment as he fell to Ignacio Buse in straight sets at the Winston-Salem Open. The British player was unable to claim his first title at this level of competition.

Reaching the final represented a significant milestone in Fery's professional career, but he will have to wait for another opportunity to secure an ATP Tour title.

hero.headline: Dolly Parton Dies
hero.body:
Country music legend Dolly Parton has died at age 80 following a battle with cancer, according to reports released this week. The singer, songwriter, actress, and philanthropist was one of the most influential figures in American entertainment, with a career that transformed country music and extended far beyond the genre.

Parton rose to prominence in the 1960s after moving to Nashville at 18 to pursue a recording career. She quickly became a songwriter for Combine Publishing before signing with Monument Records as an artist. Her early career included eight years as a television personality on Porter Wagoner's popular variety show starting in 1967, though her solo recordings initially outsold her duets with Wagoner.

Her breakthrough came after leaving Wagoner in 1974. She wrote "I Will Always Love You" as a farewell to him, and the song became a signature hit. The track gained international recognition when Whitney Houston recorded it for the 1992 film "The Bodyguard," becoming one of the best-selling singles ever made. Parton's refusal to cede publishing rights to the song, even when Elvis Presley requested them, proved to be a pivotal decision.

With a distinctive soprano voice featuring a remarkable vibrato and east Tennessee twang, Parton became Nashville's most recognized female export. Her catalog of hits included "Jolene" and numerous other songs that explored themes of love, loss, and female empowerment. Over her lifetime, she earned 10 Grammy Awards, 11 Academy of Country Music Awards, and many other accolades.

Beyond music, Parton built a substantial business empire. She starred in films including "9 to 5" and "Steel Magnolias," and established Dollywood, the theme park in Tennessee that became a major attraction.

Parton's charitable contributions defined much of her later life. She founded the Imagination Library in 1995, a program that has distributed free books to millions of children worldwide, inspired by her father's inability to read. During the COVID-19 pandemic, she donated one million dollars to vaccine research at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. She also provided aid to people affected by wildfires and hurricanes.

Known for her wit and maximalist approach to life, Parton became a cultural icon whose appeal transcended generational and genre boundaries. Her distinctive style, featuring her signature platinum hair and elaborate fashion choices, made her a fashion icon in her own right. She was one of the first country stars to achieve mainstream crossover success, playing a major role in bringing country music to wider audiences.

Tributes have poured in from across the entertainment, music, and political worlds, celebrating her lasting impact on culture and her generous spirit.

cards.headline: Olivia Rodrigo Headlines Daisy Chain Festival With Stevie Nicks, Sarah McLachlan, Alanis Morissette
cards.teaser: The pop star closed her inaugural all-women music festival with guest appearances from three generations of music icons.

cards.headline: Harry Styles References Taylor Swift Wedding During Madison Square Garden Residency Opener
cards.teaser: The pop star opened his 30-show Madison Square Garden run with a tribute to Dolly Parton and a mention of his ex-girlfriend's recent marriage.
cards.body:
Harry Styles opened his 30-concert residency at Madison Square Garden with a show that included both a tribute to Dolly Parton and a reference to Taylor Swift's wedding to Travis Kelce. Styles mentioned Swift's marriage near the end of the performance.

The residency marks an extended engagement at the venue, which Styles noted as home to the New York Knicks. The opening night featured multiple moments acknowledging both past and present figures in popular culture.

cards.headline: Tom Cruise Announces Days of Thunder Sequel With Anne Hathaway for 2028
cards.teaser: Paramount set a release date for a follow-up to the 1990 racing film, with Anne Hathaway joining the cast alongside Cruise.
cards.body:
Tom Cruise announced a sequel to "Days of Thunder," the 1990 racing film, with a planned 2028 release from Paramount Pictures. Anne Hathaway will co-star in the follow-up, joining Cruise in the racing-themed production.

The original film centered on NASCAR racing and became a cultural touchstone of early 1990s cinema. Paramount has set an official release date for the sequel, which will bring Cruise back to the racing genre more than three decades after the first film.

cards.headline: Korean Drama The Legend of Kitchen Soldier Gains International Festival Recognition
cards.teaser: The CJ ENM series was selected as the only Korean drama in the Special Screening section at Series Mania in France.
cards.body:
"The Legend of Kitchen Soldier" became the only Korean drama selected for the Special Screening section at Series Mania in Lille, France, earlier this year. The series later won recognition at the festival, marking an expansion of Korean television content in European markets.

Produced by CJ ENM, the show began as what producers described as a calculated creative gamble. The series has since gained attention in international television markets, representing the continued global reach of Korean drama productions beyond their domestic audience.

cards.headline: Cabin Owner From Heated Rivalry Reconsidered Allowing HBO Show to Return for Season 2
cards.teaser: Michael Kutryk, whose property became famous through the first season, said he needed to reflect before agreeing to host production again.

The cabin became well-known through its prominent role in the first season of the HBO series. Kutryk ultimately agreed to host the production for season two after his period of reflection on the decision.

cards.headline: Reality TV Figure Claims Daughter Rejected From Private School Over OnlyFans Content
cards.teaser: Lauryn Efird, known as Pumpkin from the Mama June reality series, said her eight-year-old daughter was denied admission due to her adult content work.
cards.body:
Lauryn Efird, who appears on reality television as Pumpkin, said a private school rejected her eight-year-old daughter's application because of Efird's OnlyFans content. Efird is considering legal action in response to the school's decision.

Efird is the daughter of June Shannon, known as Mama June from various reality television programs. Multiple outlets reported that the school cited Efird's adult content work as the reason for denying the child's admission to the private institution.

hero.headline: Carlson calls for Trump removal over nuclear weapons consideration
hero.body:
Tucker Carlson, a prominent conservative podcaster, stated on Friday that President Trump should be removed from office immediately if he is actively considering the first use of nuclear weapons. Carlson said that even contemplating such action should disqualify any president from serving.

"The second any president actively considers the first use of nuclear weapons, that person should be removed from office immediately," Carlson said during his podcast.

The comments represent a notable departure from typical conservative media support for Trump. Carlson framed the issue as a fundamental question of presidential fitness rather than as a partisan political attack. His remarks come amid ongoing discussions about the scope of presidential war powers and military operations in the Middle East.

The source material provided does not specify what prompted Carlson's statement or whether he possesses direct knowledge of Trump considering nuclear options. The White House has not commented on the remarks.

Recent developments in the Trump administration's foreign policy include a nuclear cooperation agreement signed with Saudi Arabia. Under the deal, the kingdom would be enabled to enrich its own uranium for nuclear reactors. At a House Foreign Affairs Committee hearing, Democratic Congressman Brad Sherman called for an oversight hearing of the agreement, suggesting the technology transfer could be as significant a mistake as arming the Shah of Iran during the 1970s.

The specifics of the Saudi Arabia agreement remain unclear until the full text is released. Initial reports suggest it could allow uranium enrichment in Saudi Arabia, potentially opening a pathway to nuclear weapons development in the kingdom. This contrasts with a similar 2009 agreement between the Obama administration and the United Arab Emirates, which included safeguards preventing the Emirates from developing nuclear weapons and committed the country to accepting International Atomic Energy Agency inspections.

Presidential authority over nuclear weapons has been an ongoing subject of legal and policy debate. Some lawmakers have proposed legislation requiring congressional approval before any first use of nuclear weapons. Currently, no such restrictions exist, leaving the decision solely with the president.

Carlson's statement adds a new dimension to political discussions as attention focuses on Trump's second term. Republican figures have largely avoided criticizing Trump on national security matters, making Carlson's position particularly notable within conservative circles. Whether his comments reflect broader concerns among conservatives or represent an isolated view remains unclear.

The Trump administration has been active on multiple fronts, including signing the defense policy bill and conducting military operations in the Middle East. The administration has also reportedly been pushing various policy initiatives affecting voting restrictions and other domestic matters.

cards.headline: Military leaders advise against extending Iran operations
cards.teaser: A classified assessment warned that prolonged large-scale operations in the Middle East could weaken U.S. capabilities elsewhere.
cards.body:
Military leaders have advised against extending large-scale operations in the Middle East, according to a recent classified assessment. The evaluation warned that prolonged engagement in the region risks weakening U.S. military capabilities in other parts of the world.

The assessment was directed at Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as the administration weighs the scope and duration of ongoing operations. The warning reflects concerns about force readiness and strategic positioning as military resources remain concentrated in one theater.

cards.headline: Trump administration deports Afghan to Central African Republic
cards.teaser: The individual deported was a relative of Afghans who had assisted the U.S. military during the war.
cards.body:
The Trump administration deported an Afghan man to the Central African Republic despite his family's ties to U.S. military operations. His brothers had worked in support of American forces, and as a result, the family faced threats from the Taliban in Afghanistan.

The deportation raises concerns about how the U.S. protects relatives of those who assisted with military operations. The Central African Republic appears to have no connection to the individual or his family, making it an unusual destination for deportation.

cards.headline: Kennedy Center legal battle could block Trump demolition plans
cards.teaser: Rep. Joyce Beatty said ongoing litigation may prevent the administration from tearing down the building.
cards.body:
Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio) said Saturday that an ongoing legal battle over the Kennedy Center could prevent President Trump from demolishing the building. Trump's administration raised the demolition possibility earlier this week, marking an escalation in disputes over the federally funded cultural center.

Beatty, an ex officio member of the Kennedy Center's board, has successfully challenged the Trump administration's proposed changes to the institution in court. She expressed confidence that legal protections could block demolition attempts, though she questioned who would ultimately enforce such protections against the administration.

cards.headline: El-Sayed apologizes for synagogue attack comments
cards.teaser: The Michigan Democratic Senate nominee said he regretted linking a Detroit-area synagogue attack to a broader cycle of violence.
cards.body:
Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed apologized Saturday to Jewish Democrats for comments he made following a March attack on a Detroit-area synagogue. He said he regretted linking the attack to a broader cycle of violence in his initial response.

El-Sayed made the apology during an appearance before the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus at the state party convention. He acknowledged that his earlier framing had trampled on the pain of those affected by the attack, stating "you don't ever want to trample somebody's pain."

cards.headline: Republicans bank on Kennedy health movement for midterm gains
cards.teaser: The main organization supporting Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s Make America Healthy Again movement has made little impact on Republican candidates.
cards.body:
Less than three months before midterm elections, the main political organization supporting Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s Make America Healthy Again movement has barely made a splash in helping Republican candidates. President Trump and parts of the Republican Party have aligned his Make America Great Again movement with MAHA and Kennedy.

The limited impact raises questions about whether the health-focused initiative can translate into electoral gains for Republicans. The party has invested political capital in associating with Kennedy and his platform, but the organizational support has not materialized as expected.

cards.headline: Former Republicans run as Democrats in midterm races
cards.teaser: Democratic candidates with GOP backgrounds are highlighting their party switches in races across the country.
cards.body:
Former Republican politicians now running as Democrats are leaning into their pasts as they compete in midterm races across the country. The candidates are using their GOP backgrounds as a campaign asset rather than avoiding discussion of their former party affiliation.

The strategy reflects an attempt to appeal to moderate and independent voters who may be skeptical of traditional Democratic candidates. By emphasizing their political evolution, these candidates hope to broaden their appeal in competitive districts.
